newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian rebels dig in, dish out "justice".
newsitem.headline: Albanian rebels dig in, dish out "justice".

text.p: Heavily-armed rebels in this picturesque port prepared to send an Albanian secret police officer to a "people's court" in the town square on Thursday as they fortified hilltop defences against a possible army attack.
Insurgents who seized control of the town during widespread anti-government riots at the weekend dug in on hilltops at the eastern entrance to the town, a Reuters photographer said.
Rebel checkpoints were set up and increasingly well-built barricades raised to defend Sarande against any attempt to crush the uprising by regular army troops.
Thousands of residents have joined the uprising against President Sali Berisha, seizing an array of weapons from state arsenals during the weekend rioting.
Sarande sits in the far southwestern corner of the small Balkan country, just across from the Greek island of Corfu and just north of the Greek border.
For five days locals have run riot, firing new Khalashnikov assault rifles in the air, driving a seized tank around town and sporting headscarves and ghoulish masks to hide their faces.

But former army officers, siding with the rebels, organised hundreds of gunmen into units, set up well-fortified defensive positions and established radio links with rebel strongholds in the nearby hills.

"We're telling everyone to uncover their faces. We're not criminals. We're freedom fighters who are fighting for everyone in Sarande," a group leader at the main hilltop barricade at the entrance to Sarande told Reuters.
Heavy machine-guns and anti-aircraft artillery were being placed around the position and camouflage was used to cover weapons for the first time.
Rebel groups were also moving into the hill country to the north of Sarande, where the first clash took place with about 60 army regulars on Wednesday.
In Sarande, a man accused of being a police agent was being held by the rebels and was to be sent before a "people's court".

The rebels tied another suspect to a telephone pole and kicked him repeatedly in the face on Wednesday. He was dragged before an enraged mob in the square where he "confessed" over a public address system. His fate is unknown.
Sarande was mostly quiet on Thursday, unlike previous days this week when bursts of automatic rifle fire have filled the air as boys and men alike tried out their new weapons.
But there was little spontaneous gunfire on Thursday and most people were busy preparing for a possible assault.
A tank was seized on Wednesday and paraded around town with a pack of gunmen aboard. But on Thursday it was set up behind a well-built defensive position to the east of Sarande.
A main bridge about 20 km (12 miles) east of Sarande was bombed on Wednesday, limiting access to the coastal town from army barracks to the north or from the Greek border to the south.
Four army tanks were parked on the main north-south road at the Muzine junction which leads to Sarande. Soldiers let cars detour around the tanks without interference.
The Muzine road is one of two land links into Sarande and links the port to Gjirokaster to the north and Greece to the south. The other Sarande road runs along the coast.
A deep crater, five metres (yards) across, was blasted in the roadbed on the bridge and only cars could skirt around it.
It was unclear which side, rebels or army, had blown up the bridge in the first clash between rebels and regular army troops in the area on Wednesday.
After the bridge, rebels control the area and a Reuters photographer said they had blocked the road every 100 metres (yards) with trucks or barricades.
Several kilometres (miles) down the Muzine road, well-armed gunmen stopped cars at a series of rebel checkpoints. For the first time rebels searched cars for weapons before letting them pass.
"We have a war on. What else can we do," one gunman said.
